slides.text: As a sign language interpreter for the university, my job is to be completely invisible. I channel other people's words. I was assigned to Professor Hayes, a brilliant, deaf historian who was just as intimidating as he was devastatingly handsome. For two semesters, I became his voice. We stood side by side in crowded lecture halls, completely in sync, finishing each other's sentences without making a single sound.

I fell desperately in love with his brilliant mind and kind eyes, but I knew my place. I was just the vessel for his lectures. At the end of the year, he stood before a massive auditorium of five hundred students for his final speech. He looked directly at me, gave a remarkably soft smile, and began to sign. I instinctively opened my mouth to translate his words to the crowd.

But the words caught violently in my throat. I stared at him, paralyzed, as hot tears immediately welled in my eyes. The students were confused by my silence, but Professor Hayes never broke eye contact with me. He wasn't signing a history lecture. He was signing, 'The most beautiful part of my day is watching you speak for me. I love you. Please, tell them.'
